slides.source_notes: This presentation examines how large language models (LLMs) can support the day-to-day work of an asset manager. Each topic covers the current workflow, relevant industry examples and a proposed application for the firm. The discussion follows front-, middle- and back-office work, using Company A and a quarterly client update as recurring examples. Cover image: an AI-generated research workspace.

The inputs are documents, data, messages and business requests. LLMs interpret questions, read and compare material, organize explanations, and draft text or code. Connected tools perform queries, calculations and other operations. Employees check the results and use them to complete research, trading preparation, client communications, review and development tasks.

The map covers seven application areas. Each topic begins with the work employees do and the repetitive preparation it involves, then looks at industry examples and a proposed application for the firm. Company A links research, quote preparation and risk monitoring. The quarterly client update links drafting, review and document maintenance. The task names locate the seven application areas across the firm.

The analyst needs to explain why Company A’s revenue grew and whether that growth can continue. The preparation involves locating comparable revenue and volume data, reading the explanation in meeting notes and comparing two research reports. In this illustrative scenario, prior-quarter and current-quarter revenue are RMB 100m and RMB 110m, while sales volume is 1.0m and 1.1m units. Repeated searches, extraction, calculations and rereading are the work required before the analyst can assess the business. The next three slides show industry approaches to earnings analysis, research synthesis and template preparation.

Tianhong’s FinAgent breaks a net-profit question into revenue, cost of sales and expenses, then explores drivers such as volume, selling price, raw materials and distribution. The LLM organizes the questions and calls data and calculation tools. Those tools return the figures and calculations. The model connects them to operating and industry information, while the analyst assesses the quality and persistence of growth. Tianhong reported that the time required for manual data preparation and calculations fell from days to minutes.

Fullgoal first uses the model to assess each report’s relevance to the investment target. It then summarizes the reports against the analyst’s research interests, synthesizes the summaries, adjusts the wording and checks the result. In the Company A example, Report A links higher volumes to a lasting demand recovery. Report B emphasizes channel restocking and questions whether it will persist. The LLM makes the common ground and competing explanations easy to compare. The analyst can investigate the disagreement with the original reports at hand.

Zhong Ou’s assistant connects internal research information and external sources, separates collection, analysis and synthesis, and populates a research template. The example maps financials and calculations to operating changes, meeting notes to business drivers, and research reports to open questions. These example fields illustrate the method. Analysts check the entries and sources and add their own assessment. Zhong Ou reported an approximately 50% improvement in overall preparation efficiency, with data as of May 2026.

The proposed workflow brings together Tianhong’s earnings-driver analysis, Fullgoal’s comparison of research views and Zhong Ou’s research-template preparation. The analyst provides a question and the relevant financials, meeting notes and research reports. Prior-quarter and current-quarter revenue are RMB 100m and RMB 110m; volume is 1.0m and 1.1m units. The LLM requests the revenue and volume growth calculations. The tools return 10% growth in each and an unchanged average selling price. The LLM then links channel restocking in the meeting notes to the reported numbers and preserves the disagreement over persistence. The analyst checks the references, tests the restocking thesis and forms a view. The figures and source excerpts are illustrative.

A request for quote (RFQ) asks counterparties for offer prices and available size. The task is to prepare candidate bonds, current holdings and offer quotes for a potential purchase of Company A bonds maturing within two years. The portfolio manager sets the request. The trader queries market and holdings systems and records the data timestamp, then contacts counterparties with the bond names and buying interest, asks for price and available size, and receives quotes. The trader brings the information together for discussion with the portfolio manager. Systems supply data and counterparties supply quotes. Repeated filters, system switching and copying messages are the preparation steps the proposed application can improve.

Southern’s Xiaonan assistant interprets a natural-language request, identifies parameters, breaks the work into tasks and calls database or business-system interfaces. Its applications include bond screening, market queries, trading instructions and notifications. Users review the results and confirm relevant actions. Aegon-Industrial’s Qianxun platform also captures trade information from Qtrade records, extracting bond, direction, price and size. It matches that information with the portfolio manager’s quote request and routes it to the trading system, where the portfolio manager submits the instruction. These are two distinct industry examples: connecting language to system queries and reducing repeated entry of trade information.

The portfolio manager wants to buy Company A bonds maturing within two years, check current holdings and collect offer quotes. The LLM extracts the issuer, maturity condition and requested data, then calls the business query. Systems return the candidates, maturities and holdings. The trader first requests quotes from counterparties, then provides the received quote messages or quote records. The LLM extracts the bond, clean price and available face value from the supplied records, then combines these details with the system results. In the example, the Company A bond has 1.2 years to maturity, the current holding is RMB 20m face value, the offer clean price is RMB 100.20 per RMB 100 face value, and RMB 20m face value is available. The trader checks the record’s source, time and amounts. The portfolio manager uses the summary to discuss next steps. The approach draws on Southern’s natural-language queries and Aegon-Industrial’s parsing of trading records.

A client relationship manager first establishes what the client wants to understand. Preparing a quarterly update then means finding the relevant portfolio managers’ investment views, checking product documents and the reporting period, and adapting the wording for the client’s questions. The same material is repeatedly reused in updates, product Q&A and institutional request for proposal (RFP) responses. The next slides show Tianhong’s view summaries, ICBCUBS’s RFP support and a proposed quarterly-update workflow.

Tianhong brings together recent manager presentations, market comments and periodic reports for a named portfolio manager or product. The LLM finds the relevant views, removes duplication and writes a concise explanation for client-facing teams. The example turns a view on Company A’s volume growth and raw-material costs into a client summary. Employees check and use that summary in their communication. Tianhong also turns market information into weekly sector views and daily commentary.

The model finds the internal process description, identifies the responsibilities of analysts and portfolio managers, and drafts the relevant answer with a source reference. The business team checks the answer against the source and addresses the client’s specific requirements. The question and answer on the slide are illustrative.

The client team supplies a question, existing portfolio manager views and product information. The LLM selects the relevant content and organizes a quarterly client update. In the example, the existing view says volume growth drove Company A’s revenue and that raw-material costs should be monitored. V1 is the initial draft, prepared from the supplied Q2 product information. The client team checks the investment view and submits V1 for review. The following section compares it with the fuller current presentation and Q3 product documents.

The reviewer compares V1 with the current portfolio manager presentation. V1 links revenue growth to volumes; the fuller source explains that channel restocking supported volumes and that its persistence needs monitoring. The reviewer must assess whether the update explains the driver and preserves the factors to monitor, alongside checks on the fund name, reporting period and risk disclosure. Finding the relevant passages, comparing their meaning and explaining proposed edits are tasks an LLM can support.

Penghua’s marketing-material review system applies 71 rules across seven categories and produces suggested edits. The rules cover risk disclosures, fund information, performance claims and prohibited marketing statements. Penghua reported a 91% acceptance rate for suggested edits. Yingmi, a fund distributor, accepts text or files, identifies issues and reasons, suggests changes and supports rechecking after revision. The illustrative client update shows the model checking the full fund name and current reporting period, recognizing the missing restocking explanation and uncertainty over continued restocking, and making the risk wording more specific.

The proposed application brings V1, current product information and the full portfolio manager presentation into the same review task. Document tools match names, reporting periods and source passages. The LLM reads the wording in context, explains the missing business driver and factor to monitor, and suggests a concrete revision. V2 identifies channel restocking as the sales volume driver and retains uncertainty over whether restocking continues, updates the formal fund name and source version, and uses the product’s specific risk wording. The author approves the edits. The reviewer checks the source, rationale and revised document.

The risk analyst receives an alert: Company A’s credit rating is on watch. Operating cash flow is under pressure. The next questions are which funds hold the issuer’s bonds, which monitoring requirements apply, and what existing research needs updating. Answering them means querying holdings, locating contract or internal-policy clauses and reviewing issuer research. The alert and scenario are illustrative. Peer practices on the next slide show how models can help with alert extraction, rule explanations and event assessments.

China Universal’s platform uses an LLM to extract risk information from custodian alerts and route it to the risk team’s workspace. It also links system rules to regulations, internal controls and contract wording so that a model can explain the basis for a rule trigger. Tianhong’s event assistant brings together event details, historical parallels, industry relationships and market sentiment to develop an impact explanation. Investment and risk teams use the material to discuss the event and determine their response.

The risk team provides the alert. A holdings query returns that Product A holds Company A bonds with RMB 20m face value. The applicable example monitoring requirement calls for an issuer-research update following a credit event. The LLM identifies the issuer, maps the exposure to Product A and brings the requirement and existing research into an assessment. Cash-flow pressure affects the issuer’s capacity to service debt. The credit assessment and cash-flow trends require further review. Risk staff check holdings and clauses, analysts update their assessment, and portfolio managers discuss the response. The event, requirement, fund and amounts are illustrative.

Operations teams transcribe and check fields from faxes and scans, compare client-update versions paragraph by paragraph, and repeat common edits across related files. These tasks require both moving information between formats and reading enough context to understand each change. The peer examples cover automated data entry and document comparison. The proposed application then shows how a model can explain what a change means for the client material.

HuaAn’s platform recognizes information in faxes and forms handled by its direct-sales counter and uses it to populate client-service records. HuaAn reported that more than 80% of these faxes were processed using automated data entry. ICBCUBS FundGPT supports content recognition and comparison across PDF, Word and scanned documents, with visual differences, typo detection and export. The client-update example highlights the added wording on channel restocking and its persistence. The next slide builds on the identified text changes by explaining their business meaning.

Operations supplies V1 and V2 of the same quarterly client update. Document tools align the passages and locate wording changes. The LLM reads them in context, distinguishes additions from retained information and explains the implications: channel restocking has been added as a driver, and its persistence has been added to the factors to monitor while raw-material cost monitoring remains. The change summary also identifies related client updates and product Q&A that need the same revision. Operations checks the explanation, retains it with V2 and updates the related material. Bosera’s bulk document-revision work provides a reference for extending the approach.

The business team wants to know what changed between two reports, excluding changes to repeated page headers. Developers turn the request into testable requirements, write code to read the files, match paragraphs and report changes, then investigate issues caused by line breaks, page breaks and repeated headers. The work moves repeatedly between the requirement, code and actual execution results. The next slides show how an LLM can support that development process.

E Fund has introduced LLMs into development and testing within its integrated development platform. Invesco Great Wall’s quantitative team uses locally deployed models for coding support. The report-comparison example illustrates the collaboration: the developer supplies examples and expected results, the LLM drafts processing code and test cases, and the developer runs the code, checks the result and provides errors for revision. Generated code and tests are working material for the developer to use and improve.

The requirement is to compare reports, ignore repeated page headers and identify changes in the body text. The developer supplies two client-update versions and expected differences. The LLM drafts the code and tests. Execution finds the body-text changes but incorrectly flags header changes. The developer explains that headers should be ignored while genuine content changes must remain. The LLM revises the header filter and adds a regression test. The developer reviews the code, reruns the tests and supplies the tool with a user guide. The test result is illustrative and shows how specific execution feedback helps the model support development.

The first information flow follows Company A. The front office prepares research and bond and quote summaries, the middle office monitors events and related exposures, and the back office maintains the associated documents. The second follows the quarterly client update. The front office drafts V1 from existing views. The author revises it using review findings, and the reviewer checks V2. The back office explains the differences and updates related documents. The links show information reuse and collaboration across teams.

Employees provide a business question and relevant material. Applications combine LLMs with the tools required for the task. The LLM interprets questions, reads sources, compares explanations and generates text or code. Tools perform queries, calculations and file operations, and execute programs and tests. Shared documents, knowledge bases and business data retain their access rights, references and versions. Qwen and DeepSeek are possible model services to evaluate against the firm’s actual tasks.

Research, sales, compliance and IT can first assemble task examples and source material for research and client-communication applications. Trading, operations and IT can then connect queries and document processing so that the information prepared by the model can be used in subsequent work. Development support and internal services can follow, with clear ownership for maintenance and source updates. Each phase builds on how employees actually use the preceding applications.

Initial focus: research and client communications. Compare similar tasks before and after application use, tracking elapsed task completion time, use of outputs, rework and repeat usage. Use the findings to identify whether the issue is missing information, an unsuitable model explanation or an awkward query or file-handling step. Continued use and reduced preparation work provide a practical basis for deciding what to improve and extend.
Task completion time is the elapsed time from starting the task to completing the output. Repeat usage means whether employees continue to use the application.
